The bass line and vocal melody draw heavily from the major pentatonic for their warm, soulful character

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Ionian (Major) with classic doo-wop harmonic movement
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: F# minor is the relative minor of A major

mainProgression.description: The quintessential I-vi-IV-V doo-wop progression, also known as the '50s progression' or 'Stand By Me changes.' One of the most recognizable and widely used chord patterns in all of popular music history.

sectionProgressions.description: The entire verse uses the repeating I-vi-IV-V cycle, with each chord lasting one full measure creating smooth, circular harmonic motion
The chorus is the same progression resolving firmly back to A, with the title lyric landing on the tonic for emotional impact
The instrumental section features the strings and bass line prominently over the same progression

harmonicFunction: A (I) - Warm, stable tonic chord providing the emotional home base
F#m (vi) - Relative minor adding a gentle touch of longing and vulnerability
D (IV) - Subdominant creating the characteristic lift in the progression
E (V) - Dominant chord resolving back to A, completing the cycle

techniques.name: Doo-Wop Chord Strumming
techniques.description: Smooth, soulful strumming through the classic I-vi-IV-V doo-wop progression with even rhythm and clean chord changes

notes: A: X02220 - standard open A major shape
F#m: 244222 (barre) or XX4222 (partial barre) or 202220 (F#m7 substitute)
D: XX0232 - standard open D major shape
E: 022100 - standard open E major shape
For beginners, F#m can be simplified to F#m7 (202220) for easier fingering
Each chord gets four beats (one full measure) in the repeating pattern
sequence: Strum A major for one full measure (4 beats)
Transition to F#m for one full measure
Move to D major for one full measure
Play E major for one full measure
Repeat the cycle throughout the song
tips: Each chord lasts a full measure - you have plenty of time for transitions
Keep the strumming smooth and flowing, not choppy
The F#m is the most challenging chord - practice it separately
Listen to the original bass line for rhythmic guidance
details.progression: A - F#m - D - E (the classic doo-wop cycle)

techniques.name: Simplified F#m Approach
techniques.description: Beginner-friendly alternatives to the full F#m barre chord, making this song accessible before learning barre chords

notes: Full F#m barre: 244222 (index finger barres the 2nd fret)
Partial F#m: XX4222 (skip the low E and A strings, partial barre on top 4 strings)
F#m7 substitute: 202220 (no barre needed, open A string)
Capo 2 approach: Play the shapes G - Em - C - D with capo 2 to avoid the barre entirely
The capo 2 approach is recommended for absolute beginners
sequence: Try F#m7 (202220) first as the easiest option
If comfortable, progress to partial F#m (XX4222)
Alternatively, use capo 2 and play G-Em-C-D shapes
Work toward the full F#m barre chord over time
tips: The capo 2 approach lets you play the song immediately with no barre chords
Use this song as motivation to learn your first barre chord
Roll your index finger slightly to the side for better barre pressure
Build barre chord strength gradually - don't force it
details.progression: A - F#m - D - E (or G - Em - C - D with capo 2)

techniques.name: Bass Note Strumming
techniques.description: Adding alternating bass notes before strumming each chord, imitating the iconic walking bass line from the original recording

notes: For A: Pick the open A string (5th string), then strum the chord
For F#m: Pick the 2nd fret low E string (F# bass note), then strum
For D: Pick the open D string (4th string), then strum
For E: Pick the open low E string (6th string), then strum
This creates a boom-chick pattern that references the famous bass line
sequence: Beat 1: Pick the bass note of the current chord
Beat 3: Pick the bass note again (or alternating bass note)
Repeat for each chord in the progression
tips: The bass note gives the strumming a more musical, full-band quality
Start with just the bass note on beat 1 before adding beat 3
This technique works for hundreds of songs beyond Stand By Me
Listen to the original bass line for inspiration on the picking pattern
details.progression: A - F#m - D - E with bass note accents

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: The iconic bass intro establishes the I-vi-IV-V progression - one of the most recognizable opening bass lines in music history
notes: The original features one of the most iconic bass lines ever
Guitar can support with gentle strumming or bass note picking
Establish the groove that will carry through the entire song
Keep rhythm steady and smooth at 120 BPM

sections.name: Verse
sections.description: The tender verse with its timeless lyrics over the repeating doo-wop progression, each chord lasting one full measure
notes: Smooth, even strumming through the four-chord cycle
Each chord gets a full measure (4 beats) at 120 BPM
Keep dynamics moderate - save energy for the chorus
The F#m requires the most attention for clean transitions

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: The powerful the signature chorus using the same progression with increased intensity and the soaring vocal hook
notes: Same chord progression as the verse with more strumming intensity
Full, open strumming with emphasis on beats 2 and 4
The title lyric resolves on the A chord for emotional weight
String section enters in the original, adding lushness

sections.name: Instrumental Break
sections.description: Brief instrumental section where the progression continues without vocals, allowing the iconic bass line and strings to shine
notes: Progression continues unchanged
Bass line becomes more prominent
Good opportunity to focus on clean chord transitions
Strings and arrangement carry the melody

sections.name: Outro
sections.description: Repeated chorus with vocal ad-libs fading out on the timeless doo-wop progression
sections.progression: A - F#m - D - E (repeat to fade)
notes: Repeated chorus progression with ad-lib vocals
Gradual fade-out in the original recording
The simplicity of the progression creates a timeless quality
Final resolution on A major

alternatives: Semi-hollow electric for warm R&B tone (Gibson ES-335)
Electric guitar with clean tone (Fender Stratocaster)
Nylon-string classical guitar for a softer sound
guitar.pickup: Acoustic preferred; if electric, use neck pickup for warmth

amp.recommended: Any clean-tone amp or acoustic amplifier
alternatives: Roland JC-120 for pristine clean tone

effects.reverb: Light spring or room reverb for warmth

beginner.focus: Learn the four chord shapes and the repeating I-vi-IV-V doo-wop progression
steps: Learn open A, D, and E chord shapes (the three easiest chords in the song)
Learn a simplified F#m shape (XX4222 or F#m7 as 202220), or use capo 2 with G-Em-C-D
Practice the A-to-F#m transition until it is smooth
Chain all four chords: A - F#m - D - E in rhythm with a metronome

intermediate.focus: Play at full tempo with the full F#m barre chord and add bass note technique
steps: Master the full F#m barre chord at the 2nd fret
Play the progression at 120 BPM with a metronome
Add the bass note strumming technique for a fuller sound
Practice singing while playing the chord progression

advanced.focus: Add vocal accompaniment and the walking bass line for a solo arrangement
steps: Integrate the walking bass line with fingerpicked chords
Add chord embellishments and fills between chord changes
Play along with the original Ben E. King recording
Develop a solo arrangement covering bass, chords, and melody

commonMistakes: Struggling with the F#m barre chord - use a simplified voicing until ready
Playing too aggressively - the song needs a smooth, gentle touch
Rushing through chord changes instead of letting them ring
Ignoring the bass line character - even simple root notes on downbeats add a lot
practiceRoutine: Warm up with A - D - E chord changes for 3 minutes
Add F#m and practice the full A - F#m - D - E cycle slowly
Use a metronome at 90 BPM and play the progression on repeat
Increase tempo gradually to 120 BPM (song tempo)
Play through the full song structure from intro to outro
focusAreas: Smooth transition between A and F#m
Clean chord voicings with no buzzing
Understanding the I-vi-IV-V doo-wop progression pattern
metronomeWork: Start at 80 BPM with the four-chord cycle
Gradually increase by 5 BPM increments to 120 BPM (song tempo)
Practice the A-to-F#m change in isolation with metronome clicks
Play full song sections at tempo for stamina and consistency
